Private-publishing-with-Quartz,-Obsidian.title: Private publishing with Quartz, Obsidian, and Github Pages
Private-publishing-with-Quartz,-Obsidian.content:
The default building and publishing instructions for Quartz and Github Pages assume your markdown files are stored within a public Github repository. For those publishing from Obsidian, this may be undesirable — you may have both private and public files in your vault.
The following instructions describe how to publish with Quartz on Github Pages while maintaining your Obsidian vault in a separate, non-public location.

Note: These instructions require you use Obsidian on a machine that can build Quartz. This will not work, for example, from the Obsidian iOS app.

Let’s go!
This workflow hews as close as possible to the original Quartz/Github Pages instructions for maintainability. To start you should follow the Quartz instructions for cloning. You should also set up your own Github repo for your Quartz site.
The rest of these instructions assume your Obsidian content is located at $OBSIDIAN_PATH. This path should be absolute (not relative) and point to the root directory of your vault (this is the folder that contains the .obsidian directory). When this variable is mentioned, substitute it with your value.
If you store your vault in iCloud like me, make sure your path is correctly escaped for special characters like spaces (e.g. .../Mobile Documents/... should be .../Mobile\ Documents/...). The following instructions are intended for a Unix system.
Quartz Customisation
If you would prefer to opt-in to publishing rather than have each file in your Obsidian vault published by default, I recommend enabling the ExplicitPublish plugin filter. You can read more about this plugin on the Quartz site or add it to your configuration by modifying the following line in your quartz.config.ts:
filters: [Plugin.ExplicitPublish()],
This plugin requires you add a file property of publish: true to any file you wish to show on your Quartz site. By default, any .md without this property will not be published. Other file types will still be published, however.
If you wish to exclude entire folders (e.g. your Attachments folder of images) you can utilise the ignorePatterns parameter like so:
ignorePatterns: ["private", "tempaltes", "Attachments",],
While you’re here, you should ensure your base URL is configured in quartz.config.ts:
baseUrl: "GithubUsername.github.io/QuartzRepositoryName",
Building, Serving, and Syncing Quartz
We’ll need to adjust the default build and serve commands we use for Quartz, as they rely on a few assumptions that we will break:

Quartz assumes content served for your site lives in the content directory
Quartz assumes you want your site’s static files written to a directory called public/

Luckily, Quartz is a fantastic piece of software and provides command line arguments for this work.
Building and Serving
To solve the first problem, we’ll use the --directory argument to pass our $OBSIDIAN_PATH. You should do this both when building (standalone) and serving (using --serve).
To solve the second problem, we’ll use the --o flag to change the name of our output directory. You should pass the string “docs” for this value, to support a Github Pages change we’ll make later.
Your final build command should look something like this:
npx quartz build --directory=$OBSIDIAN_PATH --o docs
Your serve command should look quite similar :)
npx quartz build --directory=$OBSIDIAN_PATH --o docs --serve
Syncing
To synchronise your local Quartz directory with your Github repo, you should run npx quartz sync or npx quartz sync --no-pull per the Quartz documentation. No changes are necessary for this command.
Publishing to Github Pages
The Quartz instructions for Github Pages deployment involve configuring a Github Actions script to build and serve your content on a Github server.
We can forgo this and instead instruct Github to publish our already-generated static files directly. To enable this, open your Quartz repo on Github’s website.

Navigate to your repo’s settings
From the lefthand sidebar, select “Pages”
Under “Build and Deployment > Source” select “Deploy from a branch”
Select the main branch of your Quartz repo (mine is currently called “v4”)
In the dropdown next to the branch, modify the selection from / (root) to /docs
Hit “Save” to the right of the directory selector
Wait a few minutes and refresh the page — you should see a banner declaring your site is live!

Your site should now be available for viewing at GithubUsername.github.io/QuartzRepositoryName
Pushing Changes From Obsidian
Now that your site is up and running, you can create an Obsidian command to build and sync without having to open your terminal.
Create Your Shell Script
First, let’s create a shell script within our Quartz repo that lets us run the Quartz build commands we discussed earlier. I’ve called this publish.sh in my local repo.
npx quartz build --directory=$OBSIDIAN_PATH --o docs
 
npx quartz sync --no-pull
You may wish to add this to your .gitignore, otherwise it will show up in your public repo.
Use Obsidian’s Shell Command Plugin
Open your Obsidian settings and navigate to Community Plugins. If you haven’t disabled “Restricted Mode”, you’ll need to do that first.
Hit “Browse” and search for “Shell commands”. Install the plugin and enable it from the “Installed Plugins” list (you may need to restart Obsidian).
Once the plugin is installed, you should see it in the Obsidian settings sidebar. Open its settings and create a new shell command called “Publish to Quartz” with the following value:
cd $QUARTZ_PATH && ./publish.sh

Note: Similar to $OBSIDIAN_PATH, $QUARTZ_PATH represents the absolute path to the root directory of your local Quartz repo (this is the directory that contains .quartz-cache and /docs). You should substitute $QUARTZ_PATH with your value.

After you’ve created this command, you should be able to search and execute it from your Obsidian command palette.
If you run into trouble with custom shells, see these instructions.
Enjoy!

Work/Misc-Notes/Morgan's-Obsidian-Guide.title: Morgan's Obsidian Guide
Work/Misc-Notes/Morgan's-Obsidian-Guide.content:
Using Obsidian
Obsidian is a Swiss army knife.
At its core, it is a markdown editor which renders in real time. This makes it fantastic for keyboard users, because there’s no menu to click to create a list or checkbox or do text formatting, you simply type and it appears :)
Files created in Obsidian are not proprietary. You can open them in any text editor. You can also use Obsidian to view markdown or plain text files created elsewhere. This is nice because it means if you grow tired of the app, or you find something better, you can move with low friction.
It is widely extensible. It can become an “everything app”, but you get to decide how big it gets.

NOTE: I recommend growing Obsidian’s functions as you need them rather than in anticipation of your needs. It can very quickly become overwhelming. Start with theming/UI, make it a comfortable place to “be” and then start driving.

Obsidian has “core” functions, which are shipped with the app. It also has community plugins which can be installed piecewise at a user’s discretion. Some plugins are dependant on other plugins. To install a plugin, search for it in Obsidian settings after turning off restricted mode.
Things I do

Daily notes + task management
Documentation / reference creation

This includes work stuff, but also things like recipes, meal plans, blog posts, running gift lists for friends etc.


Publishing
Quick file viewing (pasted images, pdf files, epubs etc.) - see Awesome Reader
Obsidian on mobile

Things I don’t do, despite Obsidian capabilities

Calendar event management
Extensive data work

This may be changing soon :) Obsidian just introduced Bases (databases, excel-like sheets) and I haven’t had a chance to play with them, but they look like a huge improvement over previous table hacks.


Mind maps / network visualisations

Features & Functionality
Templates
See Obsidian Help Docs - Templates.
Templates let you add pre-formatted text to your notes. You can do this for an entire note, or just a snippet (ex. a “preamble” or a formatted checklist).
I have two main templates: my daily work note and my daily non-work note. Command + T on mac lets you pick a template to insert.
These are glorified to-do lists, with space to jot down other thoughts or notes that happen that day. You can use plug-in features with notes. You can also set a default template for all notes, or a template for just “daily” notes. Templates have variables like {{date}} that let you adapt them to the context they live in.
In addition to templates, I have a keyboard shortcut via hammerspoon that types out the current date (YYYY-MM-DD). I use this to quickly label notes/sections. You can get similar functionality with Text Expander or by making an obsidian template that is simply {{date}} :)
Theming and Appearance
I use Minimal Theme to create a “reduced distraction” interface.
I also have various parts of the application hidden. You can customise these settings in Obsidian Settings > Appearance.
If you’re on Windows, you may find the Hider plugin helpful to hide things beyond what Obsidian enables by default.
Calendar

Calendar

If you plan to use Obsidian for daily/weekly/etc tracking, this is a huge help. It creates a calendar view where notes can be accessed by clicking on weeks, days, or months. I use the daily notes, well, daily, and populate them with my templates from above.
You can also see at a glance which days have incomplete tasks in their notes (hollow dot) or what your word count for a particular day is (number of dots). All of this is customizable.
Tasks

Tasks

You can create tasks with deadlines, tasks that recur, mark tasks as done or cancelled etc.
Some of this is overkill for me; I mostly create basic lists and then “forward” tasks between days bullet-journal style. However, it is much more lightweight than using something like Todoist or Apple Reminders so I still rely on it for ex. self reflection deadlines.
Publishing
Gist support

Share as Gist

I share a lot of code examples / quick thoughts, and I don’t always want to publish to my personal website. For this, I use github gists. Publications can be public or private, and markdown is rendered as you see it in Obsidian (minus any plugin quirks). Subsequent “publish” actions are rendered as updates to the same page, so your URL doesn’t change.
Here is an example of a gist published from Obsidian. We can look at it together and compare it to the note I created locally: Git Workflow Notes (FYI: To link to an Obsidian note, you’ll type [[ and then search for the note name)
Quartz

Quartz
Quartz lets you turn your markdown files into a simple website. In fact, the Quartz website is built on Quartz :)
Obsidian integrates very easily with Quartz, and you can choose to publish your entire vault or a smaller set of files.
It essentially enables you to blog directly from Obsidian.app, though Quartz affectionately refers to its publications as digital gardens, a worthwhile distinction which aligns with the way I think of and use Obsidian.

Vault “Sync” / Backup

I back up my vault to both iCloud Drive and Github (in a private repository). I do not use the obsidian sync service, though I have heard good things.

Why both?

iCloud Drive means I can access my notes on my phone, iPad, and other computers that sync to my iCloud account. This is for ease, not necessarily part of a 3 - 2 - 1 strategy.
Github is my main backup. I like having all the versions of my past notes, and it protects me in the case of accidental deletion.

I have a local copy of the github repository on my Synology, where I can’t run Obsidian directly but I can edit notes + push them ⇒ see them reflected in Obsidian on my Obsidian-supported devices.






To set up the iCloud backup, I chose a folder inside my iCloud drive during initial vault creation. I ran into problems with this for a bit (various files not loading, styles being wrong) until I right-clicked on the obsidian vault folder and selected “Keep Downloaded”.




My github backup (github.com/MReschenberg/obsidian) is managed by a cron job on my computer. This script file (git_push.sh, below) is saved in the same directory as my obsidian vault. I ran crontab -e and pasted in this formatted line to get it to run every dat at 2AM. It adds all changes and commits them. I have github SSH keys set up on my computer, so this happens without needing to auth.

0 2 * * * bash /Users/morganraereschenberg/Library/Mobile\ Documents/           iCloud~md~obsidian/Documents/git_push.sh



#! /bin/bash
# Date in format Day-Month-Year
date=$(date +"%Y-%m-%d %T")
# Commit message
message="Commit for $date"
git add -A
git commit -m"${message}"
status="$(git status --branch --porcelain)"
echo $status >> ~/cron_echo.txt
if [ "$status" == "## master...origin/master" ]; then
  echo "No changes" >> ~/cron_echo.txt
else
  echo "There is stuff to push" >> ~/cron_echo.txt
  git push
fi
